nameStory: Slender speedwell gets its name from its thin, thread-like stems that seem to creep and spread with surprising speed across lawns and gardens. The word 'speedwell' comes from an old farewell greeting meaning 'may you prosper on your journey' - perhaps because this little plant certainly prospers wherever it travels! Some folks call it 'Whetzel weed' after a plant pathologist who studied its rapid spread.
description: Slender speedwell is a low-growing, creeping perennial that forms dense mats in lawns, gardens, and disturbed areas. This European native has become a common sight across New England, spreading by thin runners that root at the nodes. The plant rarely grows more than a few inches tall but can spread several feet wide, creating carpets of tiny blue flowers in spring and early summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue flowers with four petals, about the size of a pencil eraser, held on delicate thread-like stalks above the leaves. The petals feel papery-thin and the flowers have a subtle, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, round to oval leaves with scalloped edges that feel soft and slightly fuzzy when rubbed between your fingers. Leaves are arranged opposite each other on the stem and have a fresh, green smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that hug the ground, spreading by thin runners that feel wiry to the touch. The plant creates dense carpets that can crowd out grass and other low plants.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Very slender, thread-like stems that are surprisingly tough and springy when pulled. The running stems root at joints where they touch the soil, creating new plants.

habitat: Thrives in disturbed soils, lawn edges, gardens, and areas with regular foot traffic throughout New England. Prefers moist, fertile soils but adapts well to various conditions from full sun to partial shade. Often found creeping between flagstones, in flower beds, and taking over weak spots in lawns.

seasonality.spring: Produces its most abundant flush of tiny blue flowers from April through May, creating eye-catching blue carpets. New growth emerges bright green and soft.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming sporadically through summer while actively spreading via runners. Leaves may become slightly tougher and darker green in hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Flowering slows but plants remain green and continue spreading. Seeds ripen and disperse, though the plant spreads mainly by runners.
seasonality.winter: Remains evergreen in milder winters, though leaves may turn purplish-bronze. In harsh winters, above-ground parts may die back but roots survive to regrow.

funFact: This tiny plant is so efficient at spreading that a single plant can theoretically cover an entire football field in just one growing season through its network of rooting runners - no wonder it's sometimes considered a lawn invader!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small speedwells, but slender speedwell's thread-like stems and creeping mat habit set it apart. Remember: if it feels like you're looking at plant 'dental floss' spreading across the ground with tiny blue flowers, you've found slender speedwell.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'creeping speedwell' by some, this name is also used for other Veronica species, which can cause confusion. The most reliable common name is 'slender speedwell' referring to its distinctively thin stems.
compareHints: Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems. Bird's-eye speedwell has similar small blue flowers but grows as individual plants rather than spreading mats, and its leaves are more deeply lobed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
